submissions.title: A Week Ago
submissions.text:
I used to rush home from work every day, hoping to see your face. Ignoring the immense pain rushing through your veins, you’d greet me with sparkling eyes and an everlasting smile, asking how I was.

But now, when I open the door after a dreary day, I step into the quiet abyss you’ve left behind. I keep telling myself this is just a bad dream, and you’ll soon be there to hug me again. I can’t wait to wake up from this terror and hear your voice fill the room.

As I walk through your garden, I feel the gentle breeze, the rustling leaves, the fragrance of the flowers you nurtured with your own hands – all still so alive. But as I step into your room, I see the dress you loved, catch the lingering scent you wore... and the deafening silence of your absence hits me.

Your half-eaten bag of candies. The book you left half-read. Your bed, and your empty chair. Everything frozen in time. Just so lifeless now.

You left it all just as it was, and everywhere I look, I just see you. You were right here. Just a week ago. And now, not anymore.

You said I should stay well, and keep others well too. If only you knew my whole life revolved around you. I hope you know how much I love you.

Yet, I have to move through life. Because you’d want me to. But when the lights dim and the house grows cold, when the sun sets and my world fills with despair, I am left yearning for you. Knowing that you’re gone forever.

submissions.title: Searching for You
submissions.text:
All that was left unsaid is my longing and desire, / The spark that silently, we tended into a fire / With your courage giving shelter to my fear / And my eyes, shedding for you a tear / To protect you from grief’s strangling wire.

Our friendship felt shallow when you were near / But flooded the city when my tortured eyes watched you disappear. / My heart yearns to put to choir / All that was left unsaid.

In the light of you, urgency feels more dire / I am renewed, filling fresh my hollowed feelings prior. / I hope to find you once more my dear / So I may tell you all the things you deserve to hear / All the thoughts I whispered to my lonesome in the roar of this campfire / All that was left unsaid.

submissions.title: So Still the Boughs All Bowed with Snow
submissions.text:
In the sea of blue spruce, I have lost the stars to the needling conifers,

And the flakes that fall in an endless squall. Where do I end and the mountains unfold?

The only sound is thrashing wind, only scent is frosty air, only sight is bitter white. Hold fast to pinprick Polaris—

Know it is the same as the one in your heart. Robin-red engine, I toil through this tempest,

And trust the tracks to carry me home to meet bleak northern sun; it climbs

Craggy rock and frigid peak while I whistle birdsong in the breaking dawn.

So still the boughs all bowed with snow, In the After there is light.

submissions.title: Boots
submissions.text:
I know it’s fall I can feel it in my fingers I meet new people and I have to repeat my name

Leaves fall into rainwater Rainwater seeps into my boots I go home, I go to bed I fall asleep with my boots on Will you pull them off for me? I know you’re still awake

My boots always wear down in the same spot: The back of the heel, just a little bit up Fabric peels away to reveal hard plastic You told me, once, you did so much walking The soles of your boots came clean off

You get drunk in your dorm And I stay sober at the bar I meet new people and I forget my name

submissions.title: So Awaits the New Day
submissions.text:
I wake up on Tuesday at one in the afternoon. My head spins as I sit up in the dim room, blinking at the ray of sunlight streaming in through the shuttered blinds. I am idly reminded of how cold I am by a draft that seeps in—carefully, as if not to disturb. I slump back down into bed and wonder how much longer this can go on.

Sometime later, the phone rings and I fumble for it, groping at the cool maple of the bedside table. The caller identifies herself as my mother, though she needn’t have—no one else calls.

“Hi, Ma,” I strain with forced vigor.

She tells me that she and Dad are excited for dinner tonight. She’s calling from a payphone at the airport.

“I’m sorry that I can’t pick you guys up—I’m really swamped at work.”

She must hear the regret in my voice because she assures me that I shouldn’t worry. She’s proud of me for working so hard.

We share quick pleasantries and then I hang up, skin prickling with a renewed sense of urgency. The reality of their arrival has begun to sink in.

I hastily kick off the sheets and head to the bathroom, recoiling at the harsh sensation of the tiles against my bare feet. When the lights flicker on, after the stars finish their dance in my peripherals, I stare aghast at my necrotic face in the mirror. I splash water on my sallow skin, trying to shock some life back into it, but the endeavor is hopeless and I give up. The bristles of my toothbrush are in such a state that I opt instead to apply the paste onto my finger.

I pad into the little kitchen, looking for food as my stomach directs me. The shelves are barren, so I don my shrunken winter coat and brace myself for the biting air that greets me outside.

I nod at the man and his dog when I pass them on the way to the store. They are as cold and gray as I am, for which I am relieved.

I buy deli meats, a loaf of bread, and some cheese. The adolescent cashier who rings me up asks me how my day was. I freeze for a moment too long before responding, “Good,” and a perfunctory “And yours?” I smile politely as I curse myself for my social ineptitude.

The sky is already dark when I amble the few blocks home. I eat, then return to bed, waking again at six. I take a shower because I haven’t in days, and the burning water soothes me. By the time I exit the shower, my skin is a red blur in the fogged-up glass. I apply lotion and blow-dry my hair before adopting business-casual attire—a white button-up shirt, navy suit pants, flats.

I wait. I sit in the living room, flipping through a forgotten novel, half-finished. I keep glancing at my watch as if it will make time move faster. I feel like I’ve been waiting all my life, for one thing and the next. There’s an inertial quality that dictates my life; recently, though, few things compel me towards anything.

I gaze over the room, suddenly disgusted by the sight of it. The once baby blue walls are yellowed with water damage; the furniture is dusted with neglect; trash and worn clothes litter the floor in small piles. Ma would say I’m not a pig, so I shouldn’t live like one. I half-heartedly set about picking up the odd junk mail, newspapers, until the doddering old clock in the hall chimes seven. I climb into my car, a sleek, dark model. They bought it for me when I turned eighteen.

I find them waiting inside the restaurant. I’m early. They are already poring over the menu in anticipation of the meal ahead. They beam at me when they see me and I grin back. Dad gets up to hug me—I accept, though he knows I don’t like that. He is a small, balding man, she a tall, well-aging woman. They make a good pair.

We are seated by a mousy waitress with a mole that distracts from the rest of her rather pretty face. The restaurant is the dim sort, with high ceilings and narrowly spaced walls. Two shallow candles light our table.

“This is nice,” Dad says, and Ma agrees, looking around with satisfaction at our surroundings.

“Did you come straight from work?” she asks, taking in my dress.

“Yes. The firm is so busy right now, we just brought in a huge client.” I hope I don’t sound too stilted.

“That’s exciting.” I shrug. “Well, just make sure you’re getting enough rest, okay? You’re very pale.” She notes the waxen state of my skin.

“Yeah, they’re working me around the clock. They’re talking about giving me a raise soon, though.” I don’t think I have a job anymore. I haven’t gone to work in months.

“Oh, that’s good. Just be careful,” Dad says, nodding sagely. “These kinds of jobs, you know, they’ll string you along forever.”

“It’s not like that,” I snap.

“I’m just saying, be careful.” He puts his hands up, resigned. “You were always so independent.”

“Anyway, how’s Mark?”

“Mark’s good. I told you, right, he’s in New York with his family for a week?” Mark isn’t real. We’ve been together for a year.

“Right. Such unfortunate timing. When do we get to meet him?” Dad winks and glances at Ma conspiratorially.

“Oh, but we’re both so busy all the time.” They look wounded, so I add, “But soon, I promise. Maybe we’ll go visit come spring?” Mark and I are breaking up next month.

The night continues much like this. Dad orders the ribeye, Ma white fish and greens. I get a small soup, with carrots and bowtie pasta. Ma worries that I’m not eating enough, that I’m too thin, and gives me some of her meal. I tell her that I ate a big lunch, the company catered.

I pay the bill. It’s more than I’ve spent on food all month. I drive them to their hotel—my place is too small to accommodate them—and we say our goodbyes. They’ll be in town for a week.

I’ve hardly made it home before I allow the tears to escape. They wrench uncontrollably through me as I try to pass unnoticed into the new day.

submissions.title: A Night In The Life Of a Lookout
submissions.text:
10:00 PM: The Night We Met

10,000 hours. They say it takes that long to become an expert at anything. But eight months at The Chestnut Residence showed me that the Lookout could be deciphered in a single night.

The moon perched above City Hall, the colourful, albeit artificial, radiance of the TORONTO sign, and the skyline mapped into my memory were only part of its singular charm. Inside, a noticeboard crowded with running jokes and mental health posters faced a glass pane that wrapped around the floor. The worn beige carpet swallowed my footsteps beneath the bleached yellow light. A wooden counter lined the glass beside swivel stools, scattered couches, mismatched seating, and oddly shaped orange partitions that partially concealed the couches. At the time, I could not understand what purpose they served beyond making the frigid room feel more crowded.

I could trace the place like the back of my hand now. But the 27th floor was not what I had imagined when I thought of a “student residence.” My first night at the dorm was underscored by little more than thoughts of making a run for it.

I can do this, my internal monologue attempts to reassure me. Besides, my first night here is going to pass so quickly that I will hardly realize where the time went. Right?

I open the “Chestnutties” group chat and watch it come unusually alive. More out of idle curiosity than anything, I check for sudden move-in mishaps and whether I should be worried too. Instead, I find a message:

“Karaoke at 10 PM at the Lookout. Be there or be square.”

Weirdly, that was all it took to distract me from the ache.

The elevator dings in synchrony with my phone. A message from my parents tells me they have boarded their flight, making me want to bolt to the airport and beg them to take me back. I glance through the fingerprinted glass, hoping to catch sight of a plane that has just taken off, before drifting toward the group gathered around a round blue couch, warming up their voices to “NOKIA” by Drake.

That evening, I may have rapped Nicki Minaj’s verse from “Beauty and a Beat” more offbeat than I would ever admit now, but something about belting prime Bieber with strangers on the top floor of a building half a world away from home made me a firm Belieber that I owed this place a fair chance.

11:30 PM: Schrödinger’s Ding

The elevator dings always grew more frequent before becoming scarce. Over the year, this cadence became a reliable way to tell time on the 27th floor.

If it was not karaoke, the gathering was probably an unforgiving round of Mafia or Uno among newfound friend groups. During midterm season, it was often a wandering soul, worn from battling calculus alone in the Hearth, passing through to ask whether those of us trudging through a past paper felt just as unprepared for Friday’s exam.

Spoiler: we did.

But Friday evening would eventually arrive, and we would reconvene on one of the cold, grey-blue couches to release a collective sigh of relief that the war was finally over. Well, until next Friday, at least.

On winter weeknights spent studying alone, the elevator would chime to announce that we had either gained or lost a visitor, with no way of knowing which (Schrödinger’s Ding).

After a month or two, it became a reliable telltale of the hour. By 2 AM, the exhausted engineer within most of us would surrender and head to bed.

Exactly 5,000 miles away, home had become the untimely video call that happened every night on the 27th floor. Once innocently confined to 10 PM, it now relied on a sliding scale past midnight depending on when the trusses began floating above my notebook instead of remaining tethered to it.

Even my parents recognized the wooden cubicle where I sat after dinner, mostly by the mural beside me and the scratched-in signatures of the soldiers who had come before. I wondered what advice CIV 2T3 or ECE1T8 might have for this unseasoned 2T9.

I had so many questions for them, mostly about whether the scrambled eggs in the dining hall had been just as inedible then.

2:07 AM: Marco?

Was it time to repaint these walls? It seemed as though the Lookout had suddenly lost its colour.

Or maybe it was collateral damage from everyone abandoning the residence for Reading Week.

Perpetual disorder was a built-in feature of life on the 27th. Usually, stepping out of the elevator meant meeting a wave of people rushing past you to get in. That evening, there was not even a hairball in sight.

Perhaps every other floor in the residence was accustomed to passing moments of stillness. Here, where the glittering horizon remained in one’s eyeline, the quiet felt wrong. It felt less like the home I thought I had finally settled into.

That night, I craved a metallic squeak from a swivel chair or the weary creak of a leather sofa.

And I realized home had never been a place.

1:00 AM: What’s Your Predicted Failure Load?

In hindsight, I am glad Robarts Commons, Gerstein, and basically every other campus study room sent us packing.

Otherwise, I would never have witnessed The Night Before CIV Bridge Testing™ in the natural habitat of its ambitious makers.

Every year, the fateful November night before the bridge was due transformed every occupiable surface in the Lookout into a hard-hat habitat. Each bridge was surrounded by four sleep-deprived students one iteration away from passing out.

Illegal as it was, the 27th floor became a refuge for the bridges and for the anxious eighteen-year-olds who would have asked a mirror, if it could answer, “What’s your predicted failure load?”

I could have sworn every workstation was throwing its own fit about how much it hated the ordeal. Beneath the complaints, the cement fumes and dopamine felt oddly gratifying, proof that weeks spent staring at cross-sections were finally paying off.

Seeing everyone cut, paint, glue, build, and break their bridges was ironically the cement my matboard mind needed at that ungodly hour.

11:23 PM: Do You Want to Build a Snowman?

My last airport goodbye was only twelve days old. It felt out of step to be happy about anything, even if it meant reuniting with the newly familiar faces I had come to adore.

The aroma of Indian comfort food and uninhibited laughter filled the glass-walled aerie. Outside was a glacial void. Inside, my friends crept up behind me, balancing glass after glass of crisp Pepsi smuggled from the dining hall.

The image felt so rewarding only because of the panic that had preceded it.

All fifteen of us had been at Nathan Phillips Square for the seldom-seen snow day. In finally fulfilling the childlike whimsy of making a snow angel, I managed to lose my phone in the bleak white depths of a Toronto winter.

The next hour was consumed by frantic searching and had surely stopped being enjoyable for my friends. Just as finding it began to seem impossible, the phone revealed itself, by some miracle of the snow gods, beneath at least four inches of snow.

Perhaps the night’s chaos could still be restored to calm.

So there we were, stealing a moment of rest after the stressful evening, level with the lit-up sky, filling our mouths with rice and fits of laughter.

For the first time, the lives unfolding on this side of the glass held my attention more than the strangers passing below.

12:00 AM: On Wednesdays, We Cut Cake

There were all sorts of cliques on the 27th: the ones actually studying in the wooden cubicles, the ones pretending to study on the brown couch, the ones choreographing to Miley Cyrus in the back, and the ones sacrificing their brains to differential equations and their last remaining ounce of patience to “Party in the U.S.A.”

But the most quintessential sight was always that one table, whichever one it happened to be that night, crowded close to midnight with people waiting for the chosen one to arrive.

Every once in a while, while scouring the floor for a place to study, I would catch sight of it decorated with cake, flowers, and people trying not to laugh. Someone would walk in, briefly stunned, and the whole floor would join in chorus, regardless of what they had been doing or where they had been sitting.

The people eventually moved on, and the elevator fell silent until morning, but the Lookout held on to the aroma of chocolate cake as though the walls wanted the celebration to linger. By then, they had become seasoned accomplices, protecting our whispers until surprise gave way to joy.

I often wondered how it felt to be on the receiving end of it.

Ding.

The elevator joined the celebration.

It was also the last thing I heard before becoming the victim of one myself.

1:36 AM: Night Changes

When you have never lived alone a day in your life, you imagine everything that could go wrong. You overplay the mishaps, underplay the silent wins nobody else sees, underestimate how capable you are, and overestimate how much everyone else is thriving when you are not.

Maybe the timeworn brown carpet that could tell familiar footsteps from unfamiliar ones was just a musty old carpet.

Maybe the couches were only furniture filling empty space, not the place that had cradled our inside jokes and late-night confessions.

Maybe the grey, washed-out walls were just walls, not witnesses to years of nervous rehearsals, bridge-building, calls home in voices thick with homesickness, and the quiet hours when the engineers were becoming.

Maybe the engravings in the wooden cubicles meant nothing.

Yet I find myself scratching a tiny ENGSCI 2T9 into the corner, careful not to overwrite the faint carvings of those before me.

3:00 AM: Meet Me at Our Spot

All your belongings are packed, and the only thing left to do is leave in the morning.

You realize that your home away from home was never found in a dorm room or in the daylight. It was found in the people you met after dark, in the nest perched above an ageing building that offered more than shelter. It became a portal to the night sky and to the stories carried through the still hours, when only the elevator chimes kept you company.

Maybe I would finally ask the honorary DJ if he took requests or personally wish happy birthday to the girl being sung to across the room. I would linger a little longer by the smudged glass and flip the camera, as if asking Toronto to hold up a sign in the darkness that read, “YOUR DAUGHTER’S GONNA BE OKAY!” to my parents.

I would let the creased leather couch bring back post-midterm post-mortems, study plans replaced by two hours of laughter, and the friendships and relationships that had taken shape and shifted around it, while the wooden barriers quietly overheard.

Maybe they had not been so purposeless after all.

I would pause before the hasty inscription, a small dispatch to the 3T0s or 3T2s who might one day sit at this same desk and wonder what had passed through the minds of those who carved into it.

You may never know.

But that hardly matters, because now it is your turn to leave your mark. Make it yours, just as it let us make it ours.

Like clockwork, dawn broke over Toronto, and the odd yellow lighting within suddenly seemed brighter, washing away the night’s qualms, second thoughts, and misgivings.

That morning, I did not spend too long searching for the tip of the tower.

It was more fun on this side of the glass, anyway.

And 10,000 hours were not nearly enough.

submissions.title: The Midnight Pact
submissions.text:
I have a friend I see only at night.

The first time I saw her it was raining hard. It was a little past midnight on a Friday and the city was plunged into darkness. I opened my window to let some air in. That’s when I saw her – on the roof of the building across mine. She leaned on the ledge, an umbrella in hand, staring at the street below. She raised her head and her gaze met mine. I looked away instantly. Just as I was going to head back inside, a light flashed on my face. She was waving her phone torch at me.

“Do you want to come over?”, she yelled, the harsh patter of the rain damping the sound.

There are certain moments when you feel invincible – like nothing could ever go wrong. Maybe it was the energy in her voice that drew you in like the pied piper’s melody, or the harsh rain that seemed to wash away fear and hesitation, but at that instant, I felt alive and ready to do anything. Before I knew it, I was standing next to her on the roof.

It wasn’t long before we were talking about everything in the world. I didn’t know her name, her job, her background and yet I felt like I knew everything about her. I knew her opinions on the most random things, and I knew the way her brain worked. The sky had cleared up and a hint of orange tinted the horizon.

“I should leave now. What’s your name? We should take each other’s phone number,” I said.

“You know how comfortable we are with each other now? I’m afraid we won’t be like that if we truly know each other”, she replied.

She set up three conditions. To never pry into each other’s background, to meet at the same spot at midnight every Friday, and to never look for one another at a time other than that. I agreed, and so started the tradition of our weekly rendezvous.

A few months in, I lived for those nights. I had told her everything – my innermost biases, the coworkers I hated, the songs I loved, and the things I despised. I felt so comfortable around her. She was the only person I could present my mind to without fear of consequences.

One night, at our regular meeting time, she didn’t show up. I waited till dawn to no avail. That’s when it struck me that to know her mind was not enough. If something were to happen to her, I would never know. I wouldn’t be able to help her if she ever needed it. If she just disappeared, I would never be able to find her.

I waited anxiously until the next week. At midnight, I hesitantly opened my window. She was there, smiling. I rushed downstairs and made my way to the building.

“Why didn’t you come last time?”

“You’re breaking our pact by asking.”

“You broke it by not showing up.”

“I’m sorry. Something came up,” was her only reply.

We talked like usual. Right when it was time to leave, I decided I couldn’t take this pact anymore.

“Tell me your name and your address. Give me your phone number.” I demanded.

“That’s not what we agreed to.”

“It doesn’t matter. What if you suddenly decide it isn’t worth meeting me anymore? What if you don’t come back and I never find out what happened?”

“Do you believe in fate? I think we met each other because we were destined to. When I first saw you, I knew I had to talk to you and I’m glad I did. But this version of me is all you’ve seen. What if we meet tomorrow during the day, and you realise I’m nothing like what you had imagined? What if this daytime version of me seems so despicable to you, that you forget all the times you loved my company? You know why I love the night? I think it’s when we’re the purest version of ourselves – free from the matters of the world and the eyes of the public. When the sun rises over the horizon, we go back to being people corrupted by this miserable world. To be honest, I only wish you’d see the best of me. We met because we were fated to, and if we never meet again, that’s fate too. Even the little time we had, I’m lucky to have received it.”

I felt so annoyed. Why did she have to be so poetic, none of that even mattered. How much could a person even change in the few hours that separated night from day. The next three weeks, I didn’t show up. I was being immature and pathetic, but I didn’t care. The fourth week, I slightly slid open my curtain and looked at the roof. She was there, sitting on the ledge and staring at the stars. Had she been showing up every week? I felt miserable and guilty. I slowly made my way to the roof.

She looked at me and smiled. It just made me feel worse. She didn’t ask why I hadn’t been coming, or show even the slightest hint of agitation. It made me wonder how such a person could be so afraid of her persona during the day.

I never asked for her name again.

We met regularly for a few months. Then she stopped showing up. I decided to break the pact and look for her. I went to every place she mentioned in our conversations and waited there for hours. She never showed up to a single one of those places. I was hurt and frustrated. Then life took over, and my busy job prevented me from thinking about her. Our nights on the roof seemed like a distant dream.

It wasn’t until much later that I remembered her again. While hanging out with some friends I realised I never shared my true beliefs. I was always deceptive, trying to be someone to fit their ideals. I adjusted and changed with every person I talked to. It was exhausting to try so hard. I was suddenly reminded of the nights with her, when I was pure, open and genuine. If I had met her under different circumstances would we never have been that close? Would the daytime versions of us be exactly this wearisome to talk to? Her words from that night echoed in my head. So this is what she meant.

I started going to the roof again. Even if she wasn’t there, it felt good to ignore the world for a while and be myself. I reminisced and let the stars accompany me. I learned to enjoy solitude. I often wondered where she was. Had she moved away? Did she find a new friend to talk to? Most of all, was she happy? In truth, somewhere along the way I stopped wishing to look for her. What if I really did find her, knocked on her door, and had nothing to say when it opened? What if I somehow convinced her to come to the roof again, but the nights didn’t feel the same?

At least now, the memories rested in my head in an untainted box. In that box, time was unending, and we were infinite. On rainy nights, the space around me would warp, and a cellphone light would flash across my window. I’d look outside, and there she would stand, an umbrella in hand and a smile across her face just like the night we first met.

“Do you want to come over?” she would yell, her words damped by the comforting patter of the rain.

submissions.title: A Fear of Light
submissions.text:
Laughter fades, and the embrace of love slowly strangles and cuts as the daylight fades from orange to red to the absence of any colour. I lay in bed, mourning the memories that had just passed, the ones destined to disappear with time. I curse time for its unrelenting march, for taking my strong feelings and moments and giving them flight, allowing them to flee.

I used to think it was the dark that I feared the most. That the after hours were so morose that my body craved for the next day to be awoken to new adventures. That the hours in between were dreadful simply because they lacked, simply because I was left all alone.

But that time is not quite empty. If it were, I perhaps wouldn’t feel so sickly. I would just forget, just rest and move on and feel fresh and invigorated and carefree. To forget is not a mercy I am granted.

Instead, I replay the minutes that I glossed over when I had first experienced them. The calling of my name, the sweet nectar of the times I made my companions blush and smile and laugh. Then come the jokes I did not crack, the things I did not say. The times of cowardice when really, I should have said something; when my integrity was on the tip of my tongue but my adversity to causing discomfort zipped my mouth shut. I subdue the awkward, painful conversations, only for them to creep up behind me when there is no sun to limit my guilt to the shadows.

I squirm. I am uneasy. My neck aches. I toss and turn and flip my pillow. Nothing helps. I am cranky and irritable and I am quite conscious of these facts. I am sorry but I do not know to whom I should apologize. I just want to be at peace.

My mind wanders back to the day, now glazed in the colour beige. Now those touches and those hugs feel forced, feel fake. Now I nitpick my every move, my soul yearns to disassociate from me and my choices but I am stuck. I am here, surrounded by noise and frequency, air that is a little too cold, socks that are a little too sweaty, and the calling of my name which now brings me to tears.

I force myself away, back into my bedroom and the safety of my blanket. It’s over. Maybe I wish I could forget. Forget the good parts too, since they are just too intertwined with the bad.

But as the months pass and the years dwindle away, I know of my fading memory and it fills me with a quiet sadness. A longing for good times long forgotten and the need to escape from the suffocation of yesterday leave me imbalanced, caught in the abyss between two unforgiving worlds.

This abyss is where I retreat to after the world is done meeting me. This darkness is what swallows me whole and tests my tenacity, my will, and my worth. And this night is what sets me free when I finally fall asleep and succumb to time taking its toll.

With this cycle having repeated endless times, I have come to question my original assumption: I am not scared of the dark. No, the monsters under the bed are just remnants of the battles left unfought when my feet had the power to walk and trot. But if I never had to stand upright and make decisions, if I never had to talk with others or be perceived, if I never had to be, then there would be nothing to face at night. I am afraid of the light.

submissions.title: Four Corners of Night
submissions.text:
The new moon was at its highest, a hanging outline of a faint, silver circle. Keenly, it observed the four people stopped at the corners of an all-red-light intersection. It was a quiet crossroad; only a handful of cars passed through it every few hours, and at night, even fewer. At this time, the only light in the area came from traffic signals and the vintage streetlamps lining the sidewalks, softly pushing the darkness aside. These lights illuminated only a few metres around them, so even though the four people were only a few steps away from each other, none of them knew they weren’t alone.

A man with tired eyes, a computer bag, and a badge identifying him as a financial analyst stood at the top left corner. He had stayed in the office long after bank hours researching market trends and preparing a presentation due the next day. He understood the financial models perfectly, but more importantly, he had an incredible instinct and ability to predict fluctuations that could not be charted. There had been multiple occasions when he advised his company to sell certain stocks, just in time for them to drop enormously in value. He was a hard worker and objectively incredible at his job; he knew that. He could always trust himself to perform exceptionally at the office. But as he stood, alone (or so he thought) at this intersection, staring at the red light, he let his tired mind wonder what could have happened if he had followed his dream of becoming a songwriter.

It was a thought that never really left him, not since he penned his very first verse in grade four. The verse was only a few lines long, barely rhymed, and was about how he hated his lunch that day, but something about the patterns in songwriting elevated his expression – like yelling from the rooftops instead of preaching on the street. Songwriting was a fire within him that was never extinguished. Even now, it existed as a small candle, everburning. He knew that when he got the chance to start the album he always dreamed of making, it would turn into a forest fire.

Now he wondered when or even if the album would happen. He had worked as a financial analyst for 20 years. It was a good job, and he was confident he could continue to be great at it. But an increasing fear formed within him the day he signed the employment contract: what if this isn’t the right path for him?

A woman stood in the top right corner. She had just come from a cafe, and before that from the doctor’s office. She saw her doctor every few months to keep herself in good health. When they told her they found something unusual in her left lung two months ago, she worried, but tried to stay busy with other things until they could tell her it was nothing. Now, as she stared at the red light, glowing in the pure darkness, she tried to grapple with the fact that it wasn’t nothing.

When she had gone to the cafe, it didn’t feel real. How could something like that be true? She had always taken good care of her health, exercising, eating well, and not smoking. They were habits that she forced herself to follow, lifestyle choices she motivated herself to fulfill. After all, there was no one else in her life who could make her do them. She was a quiet only child who kept to herself. She didn’t form too many bonds with others. Even during hard times, like at her parents’ funerals, most people who came were friends of her mother or father. No one was there for her. So in the cafe, left to deal with the 1,000kg weight that was her diagnosis alone, the easiest thing to do was to pretend it wasn’t real. She had a coffee, a croissant, and sat there for five hours, just staring out the window. It couldn’t be real; it’s impossible. As the store closed, she left and went for a nighttime walk that led to this intersection. Here, seven hours after it happened, it finally started to hit her. She finally started to understand. The weight came back, and this time, it sat deep in her stomach, pulling her down with every step.

The words of the doctor echoed in her head just as they had in that sterilized, white room. Words that would stay alone with her for years to come.

In the bottom left corner was a teenage girl wearing a black pleated skirt and a leather jacket over a white tank top. Standing at the intersection, she remembered how much fun she had with her friends just a few hours prior. They were playfully yelling at each other while playing board games, listening to pop music blast through the speakers, and eating coffee-flavoured cupcakes. It was the last time they would meet before splitting up for separate universities. She had known her friends forever; they went back more years than her memory stretched. Everything she did, she did with them: school, cabin trips, casual summer hangouts. It would be so weird without them beside her. When they left that evening, they promised they would always be there for each other, just a text away. A virtual reminder of who’s got their back. But as she stared at the red light, the girl knew that they couldn’t be there for everything, not really. There were many new things that she would now have to face alone. That unsettling thought reverberated through her mind.

Now she was forced to reconcile with the world her friends protected her from, unsure of who she really was without them. How could she know if she was ready to be on her own? Everything she had done before was backed up by them – they shared advice and stories that guided her throughout her life. They gave her the confidence to try new things. She always tried to do the same for them. They were parts of a machine, a unit that only ran smoothly as a whole. Breaking that up felt unnatural and scary. Now, she would have to guide herself and trust that she knew enough about the world, about herself, to go the right way. How could she know if she would succeed?

In the last corner, stood a university student, shoulders pressed down by the straps of his heavy backpack. Inside were four articles he had written about animals on the brink of extinction, the devastating effects of pollution, rising ocean tides, and the disappearance of rainforests. Environmental activism was the area he wanted to specialize in when he became a journalist. This field was made exactly for someone like him. He was relentlessly passionate about the environment and truly believed that the written word was its most powerful shield. It was through words that all revolutions started, the way that formal proposals were submitted, and the way good news of victories was spread. Everything started and ended with words. So, at ten years old, he decided it was his mission to contribute to the powerful words that were stopping the environment from being destroyed. Now he was living his dream.

Looking out into the darkness, he realized it must be much later than he thought. For the last ten hours, he had been in the library, caught up in the excitement of writing his articles. He had not moved, eaten, or taken a break. He knew it wasn’t very healthy to do that (especially given how many times he had done it recently), but he reasoned that he was focusing on his riveting studies and that he would take better care of himself when things slowed down. It was fine. He was young. His body could take it. Nothing bad had happened yet. Meanwhile, he managed to research and write four compelling articles. Four! How could he possibly care about his health when he was working on pursuing his dream?

The light turned green.

They all walked in separate directions.

They never encountered each other again.

None of them realized that at that exact moment, they were each only steps away from someone who could help them through their struggles.
